title: Dementia After Diagnosis: Cognitive Support and Care Planning

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with an established diagnosis of dementia seen in primary care, the emergency department or a geriatric clinic: first actions when behaviour or confusion changes, baseline and follow-up assessment, anti-dementia medicines, non-drug cognitive support, management of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) including antipsychotic safety rules, care planning, carer support and palliative needs. Based on the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) BPSD protocol (December 2021) and cognitive impairment protocol (November 2023); the cognitive-drug indication, care-planning and carer steps are filled from NICE NG97 and NHS medicine pages and labelled. Diagnosis of dementia itself, young-onset dementia and rapid tranquillisation of acutely disturbed patients are outside this topic.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The MOH BPSD protocol states dose ranges only: no starting doses, titration steps, maximum daily doses, renal, hepatic or pregnancy adjustments, contraindications or interaction lists for most medicines. The donepezil start (5 mg once daily, increased after a month to 10 mg) is from the NHS donepezil page and is not an MOH statement; memantine and rivastigmine titration schedules were not found in any opened source.

The MOH BPSD protocol licenses donepezil, rivastigmine and memantine in its table only for non-cognitive (behavioural) symptoms; their use for the cognitive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, and which severity band each drug suits, comes from NICE NG97 (page reader summary) and not from MOH.

NICE NG97 says memantine and cholinesterase inhibitors, once stopped or continued, follow local arrangements; the stopping criteria and review frequency for anti-dementia drugs are not given in the MOH protocols.

The MOH cognitive impairment protocol lists the MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog and GPCOG as validated tools (the latter two in Arabic) but gives no cut-off scores for Saudi patients and says normative values are lacking, so no normal cut-off is stated here; use serial testing against the patient's own baseline.

NICE NG97 advises telling the driving licensing authority and insurer; that is UK practice. No Saudi driving, licensing or capacity-law statement was found, so the driving and capacity steps below are generic and need local legal review.

The MOH protocols do not mention brain imaging, blood tests for reversible causes of dementia beyond the baseline panel in BPSD Appendix 2, genetic testing or anti-amyloid therapy; these are not covered here.

Clozapine, carbamazepine and first-generation antipsychotics are shown with the MOH wording (last-line, specialist use); the MOH table prints a clozapine range of 12.5 to 25 mg a day and a Parkinson's disease psychosis licence range of 12.5 to 50 mg a day (maximum 100 mg a day in severe cases) as printed.

The MOH BPSD protocol text says a patient who started on mirtazapine with flu-like symptoms should have mirtazapine stopped under the trazodone heading; this is an apparent typographical duplication in the source and is applied to both medicines as a precaution.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

Source pages were read through automated page extraction (MOH PDFs converted to text; NICE and NHS pages summarised by a page reader) rather than page by page in the originals, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Dementia is a gradual degenerative neurological syndrome with cognitive deterioration, impaired memory and thinking, and loss of everyday skills; mood, personality and social behaviour are usually affected (MOH BPSD). Alzheimer's disease causes about 60% of dementia; most of the rest is vascular dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB); Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia often coexist and are hard to separate clinically (MOH BPSD). More than 90% of patients develop behavioural and psychological symptoms (agitation, aggression, wandering, delusions, hallucinations, apathy, low mood, anxiety, sleep disturbance); several types occur together, which makes single-target treatment hard (MOH BPSD). Many behavioural changes have a treatable trigger: infection (especially urinary), pain, constipation, medication effect, noise or an unfamiliar environment, or delirium (MOH BPSD, PAIN model). Modifiable risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, depression, hearing loss, alcohol, poor sleep, head injury) are targets for slowing decline after diagnosis (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

symptoms: Progressive memory loss, word-finding difficulty and loss of everyday skills over months to years.
Agitation, aggression, wandering, hoarding, sexual disinhibition, shouting.
Apathy, low mood, anxiety or worry.
physicalSigns: Impaired orientation, memory and executive function on cognitive testing.
Loss of independence in activities of daily living.
Fluctuating attention with a brief history of confusion, hallucination or delusion suggests delirium superimposed on dementia (MOH BPSD).
Parkinsonism or visual hallucinations suggest dementia with Lewy bodies, in which antipsychotics are riskier (MOH BPSD).
redFlags: Acute or sub-acute change in confusion or behaviour with fluctuating cognition: treat as delirium until proven otherwise and look for infection (urinary tract infection, chest infection), medicine effect, withdrawal; antipsychotics are not the answer (MOH BPSD).
Grave danger of the patient harming themselves or others: the only situation in which a short, closely monitored antipsychotic trial is considered, after non-drug steps (MOH BPSD).
New dizziness, loss of balance, collapse or change in consciousness on an antipsychotic: treat as a possible cerebrovascular event and seek urgent medical assessment (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).
Slow pulse, fainting or falls on a cholinesterase inhibitor: check pulse and stop or review (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).

Unexplained rash on carbamazepine (risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome), or flu-like illness on mirtazapine or trazodone (bone marrow depression): stop the drug and check a full blood count urgently (MOH BPSD).
Suicidal thoughts after starting or increasing an antidepressant or carbamazepine (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).
precipitants: Infection, especially urinary tract infection; pain; constipation (MOH BPSD).
Medicine adverse effects, alcohol or drug withdrawal (MOH BPSD).
Noise, poor lighting, an unfamiliar environment, or activity-related distress during dressing or washing (MOH BPSD).
Untreated hearing or sensory loss (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Brief history of confusion, hallucination or delusion with fluctuating cognition; usually resolves when the severe medical cause is treated (MOH BPSD).

Low mood is the primary complaint; cognitive impairment can be the main symptom of depression in older adults; screen with the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia or the Geriatric Depression Scale (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

differentials.condition: Established psychiatric illness (persistent delusional disorder, schizophrenia, psychotic depression, bipolar disorder)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Already treated for the condition: follow the specific guideline for it rather than the BPSD pathway (MOH BPSD, Summary algorithm).

differentials.condition: Dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Motor parkinsonism and visual hallucinations; antipsychotics can cause severe sensitivity reactions; donepezil or rivastigmine favoured; clozapine, quetiapine or olanzapine preferred if an antipsychotic is unavoidable (MOH BPSD; NICE NG97).

clinicalManagement.title: First minutes: acute change in behaviour or confusion
actions: Ensure safety of the patient and others; use calm, non-confrontational de-escalation and remove the trigger if known; physical presence or therapeutic touch may help non-aggressive behaviour (MOH BPSD).
Run the PAIN check: Physical problems (infection, pain, constipation), Activity-related distress (dressing, washing, eating), Iatrogenic (new or changed medicines), Noise and environment (MOH BPSD).

Screen for delirium (acute onset, fluctuating cognition, hallucination or delusion) and treat the medical cause (urinary or chest infection, medicine effect, alcohol or drug withdrawal); this usually resolves the behaviour (MOH BPSD).

Do not use an antipsychotic for routine agitation; consider one only if the patient is in grave danger of harming self or others, or has distressing hallucinations or delusions after non-drug steps (MOH BPSD).
Rapid tranquillisation of an acutely disturbed patient is outside this topic; follow the local rapid tranquillisation policy (MOH BPSD).

clinicalManagement.title: Baseline assessment after diagnosis
clinicalManagement.timeframe: First review and at least yearly
actions: Test cognition with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Mini-Mental State Examination, Mini-Cog or General Practitioner Assessment of Cognition and record function with the Arabic Bristol Activity of Daily Living Scale; track the same tool over time (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

Baseline blood tests (full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone, fasting lipids and glucose), urine screen, pulse, blood pressure and body mass index before any psychotropic medicine; electrocardiogram if cardiac risk (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).
Screen for depression (PHQ-9, Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia, Geriatric Depression Scale), hearing loss, alcohol use and poor sleep; treat each (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).
Review every medicine for anticholinergic burden, ototoxicity and sedation (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Anti-dementia medicines for cognition
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At diagnosis, then per specialist review
actions: Alzheimer's disease, mild to moderate: donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine alone; moderate disease with intolerance or contraindication to those: memantine alone; severe disease: memantine; dementia with Lewy bodies: donepezil or rivastigmine (NICE NG97, labelled fill-in).
Start on specialist advice; the first prescription can then come from primary care; do not stop a cholinesterase inhibitor because of severity alone (NICE NG97).
Donepezil: start 5 mg once daily at bedtime; the doctor may raise to 10 mg once daily after a month; MOH usual range 5 to 10 mg a day (NHS donepezil page; MOH BPSD).
Check pulse at every review and weigh at baseline then every 6 to 12 months while on a cholinesterase inhibitor (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).

clinicalManagement.title: Non-drug support
actions: Day structure with recreational and social activities, behavioural interventions guided by the ABC chart, psychological and psychosocial therapy for patient and carer, environmental design and a steady day-night routine, glasses and hearing aids, diet and general health, complementary therapies such as massage (MOH BPSD).
Offer group cognitive stimulation therapy for mild to moderate dementia; consider group reminiscence therapy and cognitive rehabilitation or occupational therapy (NICE NG97, labelled fill-in).
Provide hearing aids for confirmed hearing loss; treat hypertension, diabetes and depression; advise limiting alcohol, and use sleep hygiene before any hypnotic (MOH cognitive impairment protocol).

clinicalManagement.title: Medicines for behavioural and psychological symptoms
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Only if severe distress or risk of harm
actions: Treat as a therapeutic trial: start low and go slow, review at least every 6 weeks, stop if no benefit or adverse effects (MOH BPSD).
Pain: try paracetamol 500 mg to 1 g up to four times a day in everyone with non-cognitive symptoms, even without overt pain; maximum 500 mg four times a day if frail or under 50 kg (MOH BPSD).

Depressive symptoms: low-dose escitalopram 5 to 10 mg a day or mirtazapine 15 to 30 mg a day; restlessness and agitation: trazodone 50 to 150 mg a day; anxiety: consider an SSRI and, if severe, a short course of a benzodiazepine (MOH BPSD).
Acute severe distress only: lorazepam 0.5 to 2 mg a day in divided doses for a short period; avoid in people at high falls risk (MOH BPSD).
Insomnia: sleep hygiene, then a 2 to 3 week trial of a short-acting hypnotic or melatonin (MOH BPSD); the cognitive impairment protocol advises avoiding benzodiazepines for sleep.

clinicalManagement.title: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable
actions: Before prescribing: identify target symptoms, rule out other causes, assess cerebrovascular risk (age over 80, obesity, hypertension, diabetes, arrhythmia, smoking), previous antipsychotic history and movement-disorder risk; discuss benefits and risks including stroke and cognitive worsening with patient and carers; document the reason (MOH BPSD).

First line risperidone 0.25 to 2 mg a day; olanzapine 2.5 to 10 mg a day if risperidone is ineffective or contraindicated; quetiapine 12.5 to 300 mg a day or aripiprazole 5 to 15 mg a day for Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies, or if the first two are unsuitable; amisulpride 25 to 50 mg a day only if all others fail; clozapine only in complex cases (MOH BPSD).
Review every 6 weeks (sooner as an inpatient) for target symptoms, adverse effects and cognition; consider withdrawal after 6 weeks; taper over 4 weeks or more (MOH BPSD).
Long-term use only if symptoms continue, stopping would cause serious harm and nothing else works; document the decision at each review (MOH BPSD).

clinicalManagement.title: Care planning, capacity and carers
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From diagnosis and at each review
actions: Many patients cannot consent: apply the principles of mental capacity law, consider the patient's past wishes and involve the family in a best-interests decision (MOH BPSD).
Name one health professional to coordinate care, agree a written care and support plan, and review it on a set schedule (NICE NG97, labelled fill-in).
Discuss planning ahead early and repeatedly: legal proxy arrangements, advance statements, preferred place of care and of death; revisit at each review (NICE NG97).
Support carers from diagnosis with education, communication and behaviour-management skills, and ask about their own health; carers have a higher risk of depression (NICE NG97).
Explain how dementia affects driving and home safety; local licensing rules were not found (see gaps).
Offer needs-based palliative care from diagnosis; plan ahead as the illness advances and avoid routine tube feeding in severe dementia unless a reversible cause exists (NICE NG97).

regimens.indication: Mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies (cognitive symptoms, NICE NG97); non-cognitive symptoms causing severe distress (MOH)
regimens.dose: 5 mg once daily, increased after a month to 10 mg once daily if the doctor advises; MOH usual range 5 to 10 mg a day
regimens.frequency: Once daily, at bedtime (morning if it causes bad dreams or sleep problems)
regimens.duration: Long term, reviewed by the specialist; do not stop for severity alone (NICE NG97)
adjustments: Missed dose: skip it and take the next dose at the usual time; if more than a week of doses is missed, ask the doctor before restarting (NHS).
Liver problems: listed as a caution by the NHS; no dose reduction is stated.

Renal, hepatic and pregnancy adjustments are not stated in the MOH BPSD protocol for this medicine (the usual patient is an older adult, so pregnancy is not relevant); the MOH document says to check the approved product monograph and hospital formulary and to start low and go slow, since many older people need only half the usual adult dose.
monitoring: Pulse at every review (bradycardia); baseline weight, then every 6 to 12 months; stop and review if fainting, slow pulse or breathing problems occur (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2; NHS).
contraindications: Previous allergic reaction to donepezil. NHS cautions: slow or irregular heartbeat, heart problems, asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stomach or gut ulcer, past seizure, difficulty passing urine, liver problems.

Renal, hepatic and pregnancy adjustments are not stated in the MOH BPSD protocol for this medicine (the usual patient is an older adult, so pregnancy is not relevant); the MOH document says to check the approved product monograph and hospital formulary and to start low and go slow, since many older people need only half the usual adult dose.
monitoring: Cerebrovascular symptoms, movement disorders, cognition at each 6-week review, metabolic monitoring per local policy (MOH BPSD, Appendix 2).
contraindications: The MOH BPSD protocol does not list contraindications for this medicine; check the product monograph.

medicationPlan.note: Dose ranges for behavioural symptoms are from the MOH BPSD protocol; the cognitive indication, the donepezil start and the carer and care-planning steps are filled from NICE NG97 and NHS pages and labelled. The MOH document is a protocol for MOH hospitals and psychiatric clinics (Iradah Complex and MOH general hospital psychiatric clinics), so specialist input is expected for antipsychotics. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: When to treat BPSD with a medicine
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Only if symptoms cause severe distress or there is extreme risk of harm to the patient or others, after non-drug approaches and a search for causes (MOH BPSD).
Review at least every 6 weeks (sooner in an inpatient); stop if no benefit, side effects appear or cognition worsens (MOH BPSD).
Maximum 500 mg four times a day if frail or weight under 50 kg; otherwise 500 mg to 1 g up to four times a day (MOH BPSD).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Anti-dementia drug choice by severity (NICE NG97)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease: donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine alone. Moderate disease with intolerance or contraindication to those: memantine alone. Severe disease: memantine. Dementia with Lewy bodies: donepezil or rivastigmine.

teaching.scope: Adult with an established diagnosis of dementia seen in primary care, the emergency department or a geriatric clinic: first actions when behaviour or confusion changes, baseline and follow-up assessment, anti-dementia medicines, non-drug cognitive support, management of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) including antipsychotic safety rules, care planning, carer support and palliative needs. Based on the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) BPSD protocol (December 2021) and cognitive impairment protocol (November 2023); the cognitive-drug indication, care-planning and carer steps are filled from NICE NG97 and NHS medicine pages and labelled. Diagnosis of dementia itself, young-onset dementia and rapid tranquillisation of acutely disturbed patients are outside this topic.
learningObjectives: Search for and treat physical and medicine causes of a behaviour change before any psychotropic.
Match anti-dementia drug to type and severity and review it.
Use antipsychotics only for severe distress or danger, in the lowest dose, reviewed every 6 weeks.
pitfalls: Treating delirium or a urinary infection with an antipsychotic.
Using citalopram with other QTc-prolonging drugs.
Stopping a cholinesterase inhibitor only because the dementia has progressed.
keyPoints: Antipsychotics are not for routine agitation; review every 6 weeks and withdraw over 4 weeks or more.
Paracetamol is tried in everyone with BPSD, with a lower ceiling if frail or under 50 kg.
Check pulse and weight on cholinesterase inhibitors; sodium on SSRIs; full blood count if flu-like illness on mirtazapine or trazodone.

patientEducation: Dementia is progressive; the aim is safety, comfort, dignity and the best function possible.
Report new confusion, falls, fainting, rash, or flu-like illness promptly: these can be treatable causes or drug effects.
Carers: use calm routines, keep glasses and hearing aids in use, and keep an ABC record of difficult episodes.
lifestyleAndDiet: Regular structured day with activity and social contact; steady sleep routine.
Healthy diet (the MOH protocol appends a Mediterranean-style diet leaflet), blood pressure and diabetes control, avoid excess alcohol.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician or geriatrician; psychiatry (Iradah Complex or MOH hospital psychiatric clinics) for antipsychotics or refractory BPSD; clinical pharmacist; occupational therapist; audiology; dietitian; social work; palliative care.
dischargeCriteria: Discharge or manage at home only when delirium and medical causes are treated, a care plan is in place, medicines have a documented review date within 6 weeks, and a named person coordinates follow-up.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review within 6 weeks of any behavioural-symptom medicine (benefit, side effects, cognition, pulse, weight); yearly reassessment with the same cognitive tool, baseline blood tests, depression, hearing, sleep, alcohol and carer review; earlier if behaviour or consciousness changes.
